05Notes

Quick guide: partitioning warehouse tables

Partitioning splits a large table into smaller pieces by a key such as the event date. Queries that filter on the key read only the matching partitions, which cuts scan time and cost. Choose a key with a few hundred to a few thousand distinct values: too many tiny partitions slow the query planner down, and too few leave each partition huge.

Cluster each partition on the columns you filter by most often, and re-cluster after large backfills. Avoid partitioning on a column that changes after the row is written, because an update then moves the row between partitions. Finally, set an expiry on old partitions so storage does not grow forever, and document the key in the table's description so the next engineer understands why it was chosen.

When a table is small, under a few gigabytes, partitioning rarely helps: the planner reads it quickly anyway, and the extra metadata only adds overhead. Measure the scan size of your slowest queries before and after the change, and keep the partitioning only if it pays for itself.
